idiom_name: skinny controller + plain service object (minitest assertions, or RSpec)
implementation_notes: Rails controllers are ordinary Ruby classes, so the humble form is a skinny action: convert params into plain values, call a plain object or module method, and render the result, while minitest or RSpec drives that object directly (assert_equal over the service's return value, no Rails boot). What replaces the classic structure is Ruby's plain object plus a method call; controller callbacks (before_action, rescue_from) are where logic usually hides, so keep them to plumbing and put the decisions in the service. Controller or integration tests still have value for the few remaining touch points - routing, parameter handling, rendering - which minitest covers from the framework side.
code_sketch:
# service: plain object, no Rails types
class Withdrawer
  def initialize(accounts) = @accounts = accounts
  def call(account_id, amount)
    @accounts.withdraw(AccountId.new(account_id), Money.new(amount))
  end
end

# humble controller action: convert, delegate, render
def create
  render json: Withdrawer.new(accounts).call(params[:id], params[:amount])
end
pitfalls: Params arrive as strings, and conversions left in the controller are untested; convert in the service (Money, AccountId) so the shell has nothing to get wrong.
before_action callbacks and instance variables shared with views hide decisions and state; keep them for plumbing and pass explicit values into the service.
A service that inherits from a framework base class drags callbacks and autoloading into the unit tests; plain objects are both faster to load and the point of the split.
